div.p: Usually, in spatial generalised linear models, covariates that are spatially smooth are collinear with spatial random effects. This affects the bias and precision of the regression coefficients. This is known in the spatial statistics literature as spatial confounding. We discuss the problem of confounding in the case of multilevel spatial models wherein there are multiple observations within clusters. We show that even under the standard multilevel model, which allows for independent (i.e. not spatially correlated) cluster effects, the cluster-level fixed effects might be biased depending on the structure of the 'true' generating mechanism of the processes. We provide simulation studies in order to investigate the effects of confounding in the estimation of fixed effects present in random intercept models under different scenarios of confounding. One remedy to spatial confounding is restricted spatial regression wherein the spatial random effects are constrained to be orthogonal to the fixed effects of the model. We propose one way to fit a restricted spatial regression model for multilevel data and illustrate it with artificial data analyses. We also briefly describe the issue of confounding in random intercept and slope models.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Usually, in spatial statistics, spatially structured random effects are included in the usual regression model to account for spatial correlation among observations made over a region. However, covariates included in the model might also present some spatial structure, and their association with the outcome might be confounded in the presence of a spatial random effect. This is known in the literature as spatial confounding (Clayton et al., 1993;Reich et al., 2006).

On the other hand, many datasets present a hierarchical, nested or clustered structure (Goldstein, 2011). We refer to a hierarchy as consisting of units grouped (clustered) at different levels (Goldstein, 2011). Hierarchical models (Lindley & Smith, 1972) are the natural statistical tool to capture the structure present in these kinds of data. Gelfand et al. (2007) extended the standard hierarchical model to the case where unit-level observations are clustered at fixed locations spread over a region. In particular, they allow the prior distribution of the coefficients of the unit-level covariates to follow a multivariate spatial process. Here, we aim at investigating the effects of spatial confounding in hierarchical spatial models. Clayton et al. (1993) were the first to point out the issue of spatial confounding. They noticed that the inclusion of spatial random effects affected the estimates of the fixed effects. Reich et al. (2006) propose diagnostics to measure posterior variance inflation from collinearity between the fixed effect covariates and spatial random effects. In particular, they propose a model that assumes the spatial random effects to be orthogonal to the fixed effects. This model is known as restricted spatial regression (RSR) (Hodges & Reich, 2010;Hughes & Haran, 2013). Under a scenario of dependence between observed and non-observed covariates, Paciorek (2010) provides extensive simulation analysis and shows how the spatial scale of unobservable and observable covariates defines the structure of the bias in the estimation of the fixed effects.

Assuming independence between observed and non-observed covariates but under a potential scenario of confounding, Hanks et al. (2015) explore several data-generating mechanisms to analyse the efficiency of the estimates of the fixed effects in terms of type-S error rates (Gelman & Tuerlinckx, 2000). According to their results, RSR offers computational benefits but increases the risk of type-S error for regression parameters, especially when the spatial range of the spatial latent effect increases. To mitigate this potential problem, they propose a posterior predictive approach (RSR-PPD), which inflates the variance of the regressor coefficients to reflect possible collinearity between fixed and random effects. Page et al. (2017) follow a similar setup of Paciorek (2010) and investigate the effects of spatial confounding on the kriging predictor for observed quantities. The results suggest lower values of bias as the effective range of observable and unobservable variables varies in similar spatial scales. Moreover, the results also suggest a reduction in the mean squared prediction error (MSPE) as the correlation between fixed and random effect increase in the true generating mechanism.

Spatial confounding has not been discussed much in the case of multilevel models. Paddock et al. (2016) fitted standard conditional autoregression and RSR models to longitudinal data and observed that RSR provided more precise estimates of regression coefficients of the clusterlevel covariates when compared with standard conditional autoregression. However, as pointed out by Pereira et al. (2020), in the RSR model, they considered the cluster spatial random effects to be constrained only to the orthogonal complement of the cluster-level fixed effects. There is no reason to expect that, in this case, the resultant random effect will have variation restricted to the orthogonal complement of all covariates available.

This paper is organised as follows. Section 2 discusses the effects of confounding in a random intercept model considering unit and cluster-level covariates. The main differences from previous analysis (Paciorek, 2010;Page et al., 2017) are that we have more than one observation per cluster (location) and they are assumed independent conditional on any cluster-specific random effects. As there are replicates available in each cluster, we show that even when the cluster-level random effect is assumed to be i.i.d. (no spatial correlation), a biased estimate of the fixed effects might result. In Section 3, we propose one way to fit an RSR model in the case of a random intercept model. The issues of spatial confounding in a random intercept and slope model are discussed in Section 4. Finally, Section 5 provides some discussion and concluding remarks.

div.head: Prediction in the Presence of Confounding
div.p: We now focus on the issue of prediction of a new observation. Sections 2.3.1 and 2.3.2 describe two possible situations regarding prediction in hierarchical spatial models: prediction of a new unit within an observed cluster and prediction of a new unit in a new cluster (geostatistical case). To investigate the effects of spatial confounding on predictions based on spatial hierarchical models, we follow Page et al. (2017) and focus on the best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP). As outlined by Page et al. (2017), the BLUP in a spatial setting corresponds to the kriging predictor under certain conditions, and when the covariance parameters are known, and a non-informative prior is assigned to the coefficients in the model, the Bayesian and kriging predictors are the same.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: We investigated the issue of spatial confounding in spatial multilevel models (Gelfand et al., 2007). We discussed the random intercept and random intercept and slope models. In both cases, we assumed that the cluster random effects together with the fixed effects follow an LMC. And following similar steps of those in Page et al. (2017), we investigated the effect of this assumption on the GLS estimator of the fixed effects. Simulation studies were provided for the random intercept and random intercept and slope models. The former can be seen as a generalisation of the usual spatial regression model when more than one observation is available at each location.

As pointed out by Hodges and Reich (2010), confounding also occurs when different covariance structures are used in proper multivariate normal distributions for random effects. One of our main contributions is to show that the bias and rMSE of the GLS estimator obtained for the usual LMM (i.e. clusters are independent across space) under the conditional distribution ( |Ä,W) are affected by the scales of, and correlations among, the components of Á (see Figure 1 and results in Sections 2-4 of the Supporting Information).

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate effects of confounding when there is more than one covariate in the model. Clearly, our simulation studies show that confounding affects the estimates of the unit-level and cluster-level effects in different ways (see panels C and D of Figure 1). When we assume that the cluster effects follow some spatial structure a priori, we obtain similar results to those obtained in Paciorek (2010), Hanks et al. (2015) and Page et al. (2017). In particular, as discussed in Paciorek (2010) and Page et al. (2017), our results show that the effects of spatial confounding on bias and rMSE increase when the effective range of the latent random effect varies in a scale smaller than those of the covariates.

Restricted spatial regression has been proposed as an alternative to handle the issue of confounding between the random effect and covariates of interest. In Section 3, we discussed how to implement restricted regression for random intercept models. We presented a simulation study considering data generated under two different cases: a cluster-level covariate that was assumed independent across clusters and another case wherein the covariate was spatially structured. Then when fitting the models, we attempted to capture the effect of this covariate by including, respectively, independent and spatially structured random effects and compared the LMM with their respective restricted counterparts. The results show that the magnitude of the bias under the LMM and the restricted models depend on the coefficient being considered. For the cluster-level coefficient, O ˛1, there was not much difference in terms of the magnitude of the bias; slightly smaller bias was generally obtained under RSR. For the coefficient of the unit-level covariate, O ˇ1, the bias under the RIR model is always greater than under the usual LMM. Similar results were obtained under the spatial case. This requires further investigation as this is the first study that explores restricted regression with more than one covariate. Similar to Hanks et al. (2015), RSR models provided higher values of type-S errors when compared with the SLMM. Section 7 of Hanks et al. (2015) provides some discussion on how to decide between SLMM and RSR models. As pointed out by a reviewer, it is easier to implement RSR when observations within a cluster are independent than when there is some correlation structure within the cluster, for example, spatio-temporal observations. Two approaches to deal with confounding of fixed effects by spatial and temporal random effects are proposed in Adin et al. (2020).

As pointed out by Paciorek (2010), RSR makes a strong assumption of orthogonality between fixed and random effects as residuals and covariates are not orthogonal under GLS estimation. Commonly, random effects are included in the model to account for unobserved structures that might be present in the data and are not captured by the fixed effects. It is likely that these unobserved structures have some degree of collinearity with the fixed effects. More recently, Thaden and Kneib (2018) proposed an alternative approach to RSR. Their approach is based on structural equation modelling techniques that aim to disentangle direct covariate effects from spatial random effects. As pointed out by a reviewer, this approach is only applicable to situations like the ones considered here, where there are multiple observations at each location. Possible avenue of research would be to extend the idea proposed in Thaden and Kneib (2018) to the most common case wherein there is only one observation per location.
